title: General Physics III — Thermal Physics & Properties of Matter
note: Substantially rebuilt around a clean, fully hand-typed 50-question June 2025 exam sitting, supplemented by the earlier Sept 2024 sitting. Same verification standard: correctIndex filled where checked by calculation; needsReview:true where it didn't resolve cleanly.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen freezes at −259.4°C and boils at −252.9°C. What are these temperatures in Kelvin?
A thermometer's resistance is 90.95Ω at the triple point of water (273.16K). What temperature is defined when the resistance is 96.28Ω?
questions.explanation: For a resistance thermometer, T = 273.16 × (R/R_tp) = 273.16 × (96.28/90.95) ≈ 289.17K.

questions.prompt: Which law forms the basis of the concept of temperature?
questions.explanation: The Zeroth Law establishes that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they're in equilibrium with each other — this is what makes 'temperature' a well-defined, measurable quantity at all.

questions.prompt: Which of the following equations correctly relates the Celsius and Fahrenheit temperature scales?
questions.explanation: The standard conversion is T_F = (9/5)T_C + 32 = 1.80T_C + 32.

questions.prompt: Which of the following temperature relationships is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Option D mixes units incorrectly — it labels a value as '°F' while writing it in °C notation, which is dimensionally nonsensical. (For reference, absolute zero is actually −459.67°F, not '−460°C'.) The other three options are all valid, algebraically equivalent forms of the standard C-F conversion.

questions.prompt: At what temperature will the numerical reading on the Rankine scale be the same as that on the Kelvin scale?
questions.reviewNote: This one needs the derivation of the Rankine-Kelvin relationship (°R = 1.8K) worked through carefully with the specific option format given — didn't resolve confidently without more context on what the fractional answers represent.

questions.prompt: A bathtub contains 70kg of water at 26°C, and 10kg of water at 90°C is poured in. What is the final temperature of the mixture? (Neglect heat losses.)
questions.explanation: Mass-weighted average: T_f = (70×26 + 10×90)/(70+10) = 34°C.

questions.prompt: Equal masses of copper and aluminium are supplied with the same amount of heat to raise their temperatures by a given amount. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Copper and aluminium have different specific heat capacities, so equal heat input on equal masses produces different temperature rises. Only the heat supplied (Q) is guaranteed equal by the question's setup.

questions.prompt: A tube contains 100kg of water at 30°C. If 20kg of water at 80°C is added, find the final temperature of the mixture.
questions.explanation: Mass-weighted average: T_f = (100×30 + 20×80)/(100+20) = 4600/120 = 38.33°C. None of the listed values is 38.33°C, so the answer is 'None of the above'.

questions.prompt: The rate at which energy is wasted by a machine is 250W. If this energy is completely converted to heat, how many kilocalories are wasted in 5 seconds?
questions.explanation: Energy wasted: Q = Pt = 250 × 5 = 1250 J. In kilocalories: 1250/4186 = 0.299 kcal.

questions.prompt: An electric heater rated at 60W is used to heat a metal block of mass 80g for 5 minutes. If the temperature rises by 20°C, calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal.
questions.explanation: Energy supplied: Q = Pt = 60×300 = 18,000J. c = Q/(mΔT) = 18000/(0.08×20) = 11,250 J/kgK = 11.25 kJ/kgK — far below every specific option offered, so 'None of the above' is the honest answer here.

questions.prompt: Calculate the specific heat capacity of air at constant volume, given that its specific heat capacity at constant pressure is 929 J/kgK and the density of air at STP is 1.29 kg/m³.
questions.reviewNote: Using C_v = C_p − R_specific (with R_specific derived from the given STP density via the ideal gas law) gives ≈642 J/kgK, which doesn't closely match any option. The real-world value for air's C_v is closer to 718 J/kgK, suggesting the intended method here might differ from the straightforward derivation — worth checking the source's actual working.

questions.prompt: 80g of water at 30°C is poured on a large block of ice at 0°C. What mass of ice melts? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4,200 J/kgK, latent heat of fusion of ice = 334,000 J/kg)
questions.explanation: Heat released by the water cooling to 0°C: Q = mcΔT = 0.08×4200×30 = 10,080J. Mass of ice melted: m = Q/L = 10080/334000 ≈ 0.0302kg = 30.2g.

questions.prompt: In a waterfall of height 1000m, the water retains 60% of the heat generated at the end of the fall. What is the rise in temperature due to the fall? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4,200 J/kgK, g = 9.8 m/s²)
questions.reviewNote: Using ΔT = 0.6×gh/c = 0.6×9.8×1000/4200 ≈ 1.4°C — close to but not exactly matching option A (1.19°C). Worth a careful re-derivation.

questions.prompt: A concrete slab 10m long at −10°C has its temperature raised to 35°C. How much will its length increase? (α for concrete = 1×10⁻⁵/°C)
By how much should the pressure on a litre of water be increased to reduce its volume by 50%? (Bulk Modulus of water = 2.25×10⁹ N/m²)

A cylindrical solid metal rod has an initial cross-sectional length and linear expansivity α. What is the general expression for the ratio of its final cross-sectional area to its initial area after a temperature rise of θ?
questions.explanation: Area expands with roughly twice the linear expansivity (since area scales with length squared): ΔA/A ≈ 2αΔT, so the ratio of final to initial area is 1 + 2αθ — this is the general symbolic relationship, true regardless of the specific numbers involved.

questions.prompt: A beam 15.0m long is heated through 40°C. If the coefficient of linear expansion is 12×10⁻⁶/°C, what is the increase in its length?
questions.reviewNote: ΔL = L·α·ΔT = 15×12×10⁻⁶×40 = 7.2mm — doesn't match any option (all under 1.2mm) even with these clean, hand-typed numbers. This confirms the error is in the original source material, not a transcription issue — likely the beam length should be closer to 1.5m, not 15.0m.

questions.prompt: If the density of brass at 0°C is 18.2 g/cm³, what is the density of brass at 70°C? (Linear expansivity of brass = 1.9×10⁻⁵/°C)
questions.explanation: Density decreases as volume expands: ρ_new ≈ ρ_0/(1+3αΔT) = 18.2/(1+3×1.9×10⁻⁵×70) ≈ 18.13 g/cm³, closest to 18.1.

questions.prompt: A radiator has an emissivity of 0.7 and an exposed area of 1.5m². Its temperature is 100°C, while the surrounding temperature is 20°C. What is the net heat flow rate from the radiator?
questions.explanation: Using Stefan-Boltzmann: net rate = eσA(T_hot⁴−T_cold⁴), with temperatures in Kelvin (373K, 293K): ≈ −713.6W, matching −7.14×10² W.

questions.prompt: Which mode of heat transfer does NOT require a material medium?
questions.explanation: Radiation travels as electromagnetic waves and can pass through a vacuum — it's the only one of the three that doesn't need matter to transfer heat.

questions.prompt: Heat produced by the passage of electric current through a resistance is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Resistive (Joule) heating always increases total entropy and cannot spontaneously reverse — a textbook example of an irreversible process.

questions.prompt: The mode of heat transfer caused by density differences resulting from thermal expansion is called:
questions.explanation: This describes convection directly: warmer, less dense fluid rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks, driven purely by the density difference from thermal expansion.

questions.prompt: The air in a room is at 25°C and the outside temperature is 0°C. The window has an area of 2m² and thickness 2mm. Calculate the rate of heat loss by conduction through the window. (Thermal conductivity of glass k = 1 W/m°C)
The convection coefficient, h, depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The convective heat transfer coefficient depends on the fluid's velocity, its physical properties, and the surface characteristics — but not on the fluid's acceleration, which isn't a factor in the standard convection models.

questions.prompt: The operating temperature of a tungsten filament in an incandescent lamp is 3540K, and its emissivity is 0.50. Find the surface area of the filament needed for a 100W lamp. (σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴)

topics.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases & Gas Laws

questions.prompt: Calculate the gas constant per unit mass of hydrogen. (Molar mass of H₂ ≈ 2.016 g/mol)
questions.explanation: Specific gas constant = R_universal/molar mass = 8.314/0.002016 ≈ 4124 J/kgK, closest to 4.13×10³.

questions.prompt: One mole of a monatomic gas has an initial internal energy of 3.7×10⁴ J. What is the total internal energy of one mole of a diatomic gas at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: Monatomic internal energy = (3/2)nRT; diatomic = (5/2)nRT. At the same temperature, U_diatomic = U_monatomic × (5/3) = 3.7×10⁴ × 5/3 ≈ 6.17×10⁴ J.

questions.prompt: If the temperature of a gas increases from 20°C to 40°C, by what factor (percentage) does its root-mean-square speed increase?
questions.explanation: v_rms ∝ √T (absolute temperature). Using Kelvin: √(313.15/293.15) ≈ 1.034, an increase of about 3.4% — closest to 3%.

questions.prompt: Which of the following postulates of the kinetic theory of gases is NOT correct?
options: There are a large number of molecules moving randomly with a variety of speeds
The molecules are, on average, far apart with negligible size compared to the distances between them
The molecules interact with one another during ordinary motion
Collisions between molecules and with the vessel walls are perfectly inelastic
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory assumes molecules do NOT interact except during brief, instantaneous collisions — they otherwise move freely without ongoing interaction. Saying they 'interact during ordinary motion' contradicts the core model. (Note: option D describing collisions as perfectly INELASTIC is also wrong under standard kinetic theory, which assumes perfectly ELASTIC collisions — this question may have more than one flawed statement.)
questions.reviewNote: Both option C and option D look like they violate standard kinetic theory assumptions. Leaning toward C as the intended answer since it's the more direct contradiction, but this is worth double-checking against the source's actual key.

questions.prompt: For a diatomic gas, the total internal energy is given as:
questions.explanation: A diatomic gas has 5 degrees of freedom (3 translational + 2 rotational), giving total internal energy U = (5/2)nRT.

questions.prompt: Which of the following temperatures is the highest?
questions.explanation: Converting all to Celsius for comparison: 100K ≈ −173°C. −13°F ≈ −25°C. 200°R ≈ −162°C. −32°C stays −32°C. The highest is −25°C, i.e. −13°F.

questions.prompt: Which of the following gives the dimension of the coefficient of viscosity?
questions.explanation: Viscosity relates shear stress to velocity gradient: η = F·L/(A·v). Dimensionally this works out to ML⁻¹T⁻¹.

questions.prompt: By what percentage does the r.m.s. speed of gas molecules increase if the temperature of the gas increases from 30°C to 50°C?
questions.explanation: v_rms ∝ √T. √(323.15/303.15) ≈ 1.032, an increase of about 3.2%.

questions.prompt: Nitrogen molecules (N₂, a diatomic gas) have how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: A diatomic molecule has 3 translational + 2 rotational degrees of freedom = 5 total (at ordinary temperatures, before vibrational modes activate).

questions.prompt: What is the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule in a gas at 37°C?
questions.explanation: Average translational KE per molecule = (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant. At T=310.15K: (3/2)(1.38×10⁻²³)(310.15) ≈ 6.42×10⁻²¹ J.

questions.prompt: An ideal gas in a container of volume 1000cm³ at 20°C has a pressure of 1.00×10⁵ N/m². Determine the number of moles of gas in the container. (R = 8.314 J/mol·K)
A gas expands isothermally at a constant temperature of 310K from an initial volume of 12L to a final volume of 19L (1 mole of gas). How much work is done by the gas during the expansion?
questions.explanation: For isothermal expansion: W = nRT·ln(V₂/V₁) = 1×8.314×310×ln(19/12) ≈ 1184 J, closest to 1,180 J.

questions.prompt: The second law of thermodynamics is also referred to as:
options: An impossibility according to the first law
An impossibility according to the third law
questions.explanation: The second law is fundamentally statistical — it describes the overwhelmingly probable direction of spontaneous processes (entropy increase), not an absolute deterministic rule.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a stage of a Carnot engine cycle?
questions.explanation: The Carnot cycle consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes — an isobaric (constant-pressure) stage is not part of the ideal Carnot cycle.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a heat engine?
options: It converts heat supplied at a high temperature into work while rejecting some heat to a low-temperature reservoir
It uses work to transfer heat from a low-temperature region to a high-temperature region
By doing work, the engine increases the heat in the surroundings
The engine is exhausted at a high temperature
questions.explanation: A heat engine's defining behavior: take in heat from a hot reservoir, convert some of it to useful work, and reject the rest to a cold reservoir — it can never convert 100% of input heat to work (this is a Second Law consequence). Option B actually describes a refrigerator/heat pump, the reverse process.

questions.prompt: For an adiabatic process, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: 'Adiabatic' means no heat exchange with the surroundings — by definition, dQ = 0. (From the first law dU=dQ−dW, this then gives dU=−dW, which is also true, but dQ=0 is the defining condition itself.)

questions.prompt: Which of the following gives the basic components of a heat engine?
questions.explanation: A heat engine needs a hot source to draw heat from, a cold sink to reject heat to, and insulation/a working substance to carry out the cycle between them — all three components together.

questions.prompt: "All reversible heat engines working between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency, irrespective of the working substance." This statement is known as:
questions.explanation: This is the direct statement of Carnot's theorem, which establishes the Carnot efficiency as the theoretical maximum for any engine operating between two given temperatures.

questions.prompt: 1kg of liquid water at 373K is converted to steam at 100°C by boiling at standard atmospheric pressure. The volume changes from 10⁻³m³ (liquid) to 1.671m³ (steam). What is the change in the system's internal energy? (Lᵥ = 2,265 kJ/kg, 1 atm = 1.01×10⁵ N/m²)
questions.explanation: Heat absorbed: Q = mLᵥ = 2265 kJ. Work done by the expansion: W = PΔV = 1.01×10⁵ × (1.671 − 0.001) = 168.7 kJ. ΔU = Q − W = 2265 − 168.7 = 2096 kJ.

questions.prompt: A reversible engine takes heat from a reservoir at 527°C and rejects heat to a sink at 127°C. How many calories per second must it take from the reservoir to produce useful work at a rate of 750W? (1W = 0.239 cal/s)
questions.reviewNote: Using the Carnot efficiency between 800K and 400K (eff=0.5), the heat drawn from the reservoir works out to about 358.6 cal/s — closest to but not exactly matching 335.80 cal/s. Worth a careful re-derivation to see where the small gap comes from.

questions.prompt: 75J of work is done on a system containing 30kg of water by stirring with a paddle wheel, while 63J of heat is removed. What is the change in internal energy of the system?
questions.explanation: ΔU = Q − W, where W is work done BY the system. Here work is done ON the system (+75J) and heat is removed (−63J): ΔU = −63 − (−75) = +12J.

questions.prompt: The high- and low-temperature reservoirs of a heat engine operating at a relative efficiency of 48% are at 600K and 200K respectively. Find the Carnot efficiency and the actual thermal efficiency.
questions.reviewNote: Carnot efficiency = 1−(200/600) ≈ 66.7%. 'Relative efficiency' of 48% likely means actual/Carnot = 0.48, giving actual ≈ 32% — doesn't cleanly match option D (45.8% and 21.98%). The exact definition of 'relative efficiency' intended here needs clarifying.

questions.prompt: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is 75%. If the temperature of the sink is 300K, find the temperature of the heat source.
For an ideal gas, the work done in an isothermal process is given as:
questions.explanation: For an isothermal ideal-gas process, W = ∫P dV with P = nRT/V, which gives W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁). W = P(V₂ − V₁) is for constant pressure, and nCᵥ(T₂ − T₁) is the change in internal energy.
questions.sourceNote: Options and key corrected against the original paper (an earlier version had reconstructed options).

questions.prompt: An ideal gas heat engine operates on a Carnot cycle between 227°C and 127°C. It absorbs 6×10⁵ J of heat at the high temperature. Find the amount of heat converted into work.
questions.explanation: Carnot efficiency = 1 − (400/500) = 0.2. Work = efficiency × Q_h = 0.2×6×10⁵ = 1.2×10⁵ J.

questions.prompt: A force of 5N acts on a 10kg object. If the force acts on an aluminium cube with sides of 15cm, what is the resulting stress?
questions.explanation: Stress = Force/Area = 5/(0.15²) = 5/0.0225 ≈ 222.2 N/m².

questions.prompt: Which of the following elastic moduli is associated with a rigid body's resistance to shear deformation?
questions.explanation: Shear modulus specifically measures resistance to shape-changing deformation where layers slide relative to each other (like pushing the top of a book sideways) — that's shear, distinct from Young's modulus (stretching) or Bulk modulus (uniform compression).

questions.prompt: The elastic limit of a piece of steel wire is 2.70×10⁹ Pa. What is the maximum speed at which transverse wave pulses can propagate along this wire before this stress is exceeded? (Density of steel = 7.86×10³ kg/m³)
questions.explanation: Wave speed in a stressed wire: v = √(stress/density) = √(2.70×10⁹/7.86×10³) ≈ 586 m/s.

topics.title: Fluid Properties — Surface Tension & Phase Behavior

questions.prompt: In which phase can water and steam coexist in equilibrium?
questions.reviewNote: None of the given options directly names the correct phase pairing (liquid-vapor equilibrium along the boiling curve, sometimes called the 'saturation' condition) — worth checking if an option was mistranscribed.

questions.prompt: For a liquid to wet the walls of a container, which relationship between cohesion and adhesion must hold?
options: Cohesion and adhesion are equal to unity
questions.explanation: A liquid wets a surface (spreads and clings to it) when adhesive forces (liquid-to-surface attraction) exceed cohesive forces (liquid-to-itself attraction) — meaning cohesion must be LESS than adhesion.

questions.prompt: At the interface between a liquid and a solid surface, surface tension effects arise as a result of:
questions.explanation: Surface tension at an interface is the net result of both cohesive forces (within the liquid) and adhesive forces (between liquid and solid) acting together — neither alone fully explains the observed behavior.

questions.prompt: Mercury is chosen as a thermometric liquid because of which combination of properties? (I) Easily visible. (II) Nearly uniform coefficient of expansion over a wide range. (III) Does not wet glass. (IV) Good conductor of heat.
questions.explanation: Mercury's key thermometric properties are being easily visible (I), expanding uniformly over a wide range (II), and not wetting/sticking to the glass (III) — its thermal conductivity (IV) isn't actually why it's chosen, since the thermometer works via volume expansion, not heat conduction speed.
